slides.title: One DSD People, Access and Culture
slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Understanding White Privilege

Examining racial advantage in DSD service access, workplace culture, and institutional practice.

Self-directed Foundation learning for all staff
slides.narration: An ordinary practice can be easier to navigate for some people than for others, even when nobody announces an intention to exclude. This course examines a particular form of that advantage: advantages associated with being perceived as white. Your own experience may include effort, disability, hardship, and belonging. None needs to be set aside to consider how race can also matter. As you move through the course, you will examine service and employee situations, make choices, and read explanations. Community engagement and culture briefs will help you consider perspectives missing from a familiar account. The examples teach a way of reasoning; they do not establish findings about DSD or anyone in it.

slides.title: Learning focus
slides.text:
Learning focus

White privilege describes advantages associated with being perceived as white in a society shaped by racial inequality. It can coexist with effort, hardship, and disability.

Trace how an action can affect access or recognition, then ask what happens when the practice repeats.

Use community perspectives and evidence to compare a more equitable response.
slides.narration: You are looking at both the person’s experience and the practice around it. A missed opportunity may begin with one invitation, but repeated invitations to the same circle can shape who gains experience and later appears ready for advancement. In services, a credibility judgment can influence whose question receives explanation and whose concern enters the record. The course will help you explain those connections without treating a possibility as proof. Keep three questions in mind: what action is described, what barrier or advantage could follow, and what information would clarify whether race contributes to the pattern? You can apply the questions privately to a practice case or to an appropriate practice within your responsibility.

slides.title: Learning with care
slides.text:
Learning with care

Learn at your own pace and explore the examples in a way that works for you.

You do not need to disclose personal harm, defend your identity, or speak for a racial group.

Notice when a familiar practice feels fair to you. What might someone with a different experience need you to examine?
slides.narration: You can take this subject seriously while approaching yourself and other people with care. You do not need to prove that your life has been easy, describe a painful experience, or reach a judgment about a colleague. Begin with a small reflection: when has a rule, relationship, or explanation helped you find your way? Consider what someone without that access might encounter. The point is to notice a condition, not rank people’s lives. Later examples will ask specifically how racial advantage could operate. If a question is difficult, return to the facts supplied and read the feedback before continuing. Personal reflection can remain private.

slides.title: Understanding race
slides.text:
Understanding race

Race is a social category with real consequences for treatment, access, and opportunity.

A racial category cannot establish an individual’s abilities, beliefs, or priorities.

Pause: whose account is readily believed in a service conversation, and what could happen if that judgment becomes a routine?
slides.narration: Race matters because of social history and the ways people and institutions respond to it. It does not provide a personal profile. Consider the question on this slide before moving on. If one person is asked for extra proof while another receives the benefit of the doubt, the immediate burden differs. When that response repeats through a service process, it could influence whose requests move forward and whose concerns are heard. The question does not supply evidence of a racial pattern. It helps you identify the action, its possible consequence, and the comparison you would need. The next practice lets you examine racial advantage while keeping other hardships visible.

slides.title: Practice: hardship and racial advantage
slides.text:
Practice: hardship and racial advantage

A service participant says, “I have a disability and struggled financially, so racial advantage cannot apply to me.” A colleague suggests setting the racial concern aside. What keeps the inquiry useful?

A. Explain that those hardships are irrelevant.

B. Acknowledge the hardship and examine the specific racial barrier being discussed.

C. Compare everyone’s hardship until the group agrees who struggled most.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Explain that those hardships are irrelevant.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Acknowledge the hardship and examine the specific racial barrier being discussed.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Compare everyone’s hardship until the group agrees who struggled most.

slides.narration:
A service participant says, “I have a disability and struggled financially, so racial advantage cannot apply to me.” A colleague suggests setting the racial concern aside. What keeps the inquiry useful?

Choose a response, then read its explanation. Before choosing, consider the action described, the barrier or advantage it could create, and what might happen if the same response became routine. Keep the facts provided separate from the evidence still needed. You can reconsider your choice after reading the feedback.

slides.title: Another way to consider this
slides.text:
Another way to consider this

Dismissing hardship can close inquiry. Repeated dismissal may keep intersecting experiences out of service decisions. Recognize disability and financial hardship, then examine the racial concern. Neither hardship nor its dismissal establishes whether a racial barrier exists.

What service barrier could remain if racial concerns were routinely set aside?

Try another response

Continue learning
slides.narration:
Dismissing hardship can make a person feel unheard and close the inquiry. Repeated dismissal can make it harder for intersecting experiences to enter service decisions. Acknowledge disability and financial hardship, then examine the specific racial concern. Their presence does not establish whether a racial barrier exists, and their dismissal cannot resolve it.

What service barrier could remain if racial concerns were routinely set aside? Your reflection can remain private. Follow the reasoning from the immediate action to a possible repeated effect, then identify what would support or challenge that explanation.

slides.title: Why this response helps
slides.text:
Why this response helps

Acknowledge hardship and keep the racial concern open. Repeated deflection could preserve unequal access. Ask how the practice works and examine evidence. Hardship and racial advantage can coexist; this exchange does not establish a local racial pattern.

What service barrier could remain if racial concerns were routinely set aside?

Continue learning
slides.narration:
Acknowledging hardship keeps the person’s experience visible while allowing examination of the racial concern. Setting that concern aside could leave a barrier unexamined; repeated deflection could preserve unequal treatment or access. Ask about the actual practice and relevant evidence. Hardship and racial advantage can coexist, but this example does not establish a local racial pattern.

What service barrier could remain if racial concerns were routinely set aside? Your reflection can remain private. Follow the reasoning from the immediate action to a possible repeated effect, then identify what would support or challenge that explanation.

slides.title: Another way to consider this
slides.text:
Another way to consider this

Ranking hardship diverts attention from the practice. Repeated comparisons can leave racial barriers unexamined unless someone proves greater suffering. Recognize hardship without ranking it, then examine access and treatment. The case does not establish whether race caused a difference.

What service barrier could remain if racial concerns were routinely set aside?

Try another response

Continue learning
slides.narration:
Ranking hardship shifts attention away from the practice. It can leave the reported racial barrier unexplored, and repeated comparisons can make equity concerns seem worthy only when someone proves greater suffering. Recognize hardship without comparison, then examine access or treatment. The case does not tell you whether race caused a difference; it identifies a question worth investigating.

What service barrier could remain if racial concerns were routinely set aside? Your reflection can remain private. Follow the reasoning from the immediate action to a possible repeated effect, then identify what would support or challenge that explanation.

slides.title: Understanding ethnicity
slides.text:
Understanding ethnicity

Ethnicity can involve heritage, language, traditions, history, and community relationships. It is not interchangeable with race.

Culture briefs provide background and questions, not an individual profile.

Let people describe the identities and preferences relevant to their own situation.
slides.narration: People who share a language or heritage can differ in relationships, disability experience, beliefs, and priorities. A culture brief may introduce history and community institutions you have not considered. It cannot tell you how a particular person understands support or wishes to participate. Using a brief as a profile can turn learning into a service or staffing shortcut. For example, expecting a colleague to interpret or represent a community may add work and restrict their development opportunities. Use the brief to prepare an open question, then hear the person’s answer. Community learning is a shared responsibility, not a duty assigned because of an employee’s identity.

slides.title: Related ideas
slides.text:
Related ideas

Stereotype: a broad assumption about a group. Prejudice: a group-based judgment or attitude.

Discrimination concerns unequal treatment. Racism involves racial beliefs and practices that sustain unequal treatment or opportunity.

White privilege directs attention to racial advantage, including advantages within ordinary routines.
slides.narration: These ideas overlap, but they help you ask different questions. An assumption about a group is not the same evidence as an action, and an action is not the same evidence as a repeated institutional pattern. White privilege asks where racial advantage may be carried through access, credibility, expectations, or networks. An openly hostile statement is not required for a routine to preserve unequal access. Equally, one difference does not tell you its complete cause. When you examine a case, identify the concern precisely. That makes it easier to consider relevant evidence and an appropriate response without treating identity as a complete explanation.

slides.title: Individual treatment and systemic patterns
slides.text:
Individual treatment and systemic patterns

An incident and a repeated institutional pattern need related but distinct inquiry.

Trace the action, its possible effect, and the process that could make it recur.

Address the immediate concern while preserving appropriate reporting options; broader evidence can help examine a racial pattern.
slides.narration: Suppose a person’s service concern is dismissed. Listening and clarifying the concern can be useful immediately; the person does not have to prove a division-wide pattern to deserve consideration. To understand a broader inequity, examine comparable encounters and the conditions around them. Did the same standard apply? Were communication needs addressed? Whose account entered the record, and what happened next? Repeated credibility discounts could affect how a service develops or who reaches it. Community accounts can reveal questions the records miss. Keep those accounts particular, protect privacy, and distinguish a possible explanation from a supported finding. A learning activity does not replace a required response or reporting process.

slides.title: Understanding white privilege
slides.text:
Understanding white privilege

White privilege describes advantages associated with being perceived as white in a society shaped by racial inequality.

A person may benefit without choosing or noticing the advantage.

Ask which racial barrier is less likely to be encountered and which routine could preserve that difference.
slides.narration: The concept concerns a specific kind of advantage, not a judgment that every white person has an easy life. A person can work hard, face disability or financial hardship, and still avoid a particular racial barrier. In services, racial advantage might concern whose account is presumed credible. In the employee life cycle, it might concern familiarity with influential networks or expectations treated as normal. Your task is to understand the relevant practice and what it makes possible. Look for evidence about the route, the criteria, and people’s experiences. Neither stated good intentions nor one person’s hardship settles how race operates in the situation.

slides.title: Advantages that can go unnoticed
slides.text:
Advantages that can go unnoticed

Racial advantage may appear in assumed credibility, representation, established networks, or freedom from stereotypes.

A familiar route to information can become a route to experience and influence.

Ask who can use that route and what evidence would clarify a racial pattern.
slides.narration: An advantage can feel ordinary when you have rarely needed to question it. An employee might hear about development through a familiar network, gain experience, and later receive credit for readiness. Someone outside that route may never have the same chance to demonstrate capability. A similar issue occurs when service information reaches only established contacts. Before making a racial conclusion, examine who was reached, how the route worked, and other relevant conditions. Community voices can help reveal missing routes, while recruitment and onboarding accounts can show what employees were expected to know. The next practice follows one opportunity through that longer chain.

slides.title: Practice: access across employment
slides.text:
Practice: access across employment

A development assignment reaches an informal circle before other employees hear about it. Later, that experience supports advancement. What is established?

A. The invitation created unequal access to information; a racial pattern requires further evidence.

B. The example alone proves which racial groups benefited and why.

C. There is no inequity unless someone intended to exclude others.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. The invitation created unequal access to information; a racial pattern requires further evidence.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. The example alone proves which racial groups benefited and why.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. There is no inequity unless someone intended to exclude others.

slides.narration:
A development assignment reaches an informal circle before other employees hear about it. Later, that experience supports advancement. What is established?

Choose a response, then read its explanation. Before choosing, consider the action described, the barrier or advantage it could create, and what might happen if the same response became routine. Keep the facts provided separate from the evidence still needed. You can reconsider your choice after reading the feedback.

slides.title: Why this response helps
slides.text:
Why this response helps

Uneven information is visible. Early access can create experience later used in advancement; repetition can keep opportunity in one circle. Compare invitations, criteria, support, and participation, then clarify the route. Whether racial advantage shapes the pattern needs evidence.

How could early access shape later advancement, and what would you examine?

Continue learning
slides.narration:
The uneven information route is visible. Early access can produce experience that later counts toward advancement; repeated use can keep opportunity within the same circle. Compare invitations, criteria, support, and participation, then consider a clearer route. A racial pattern remains an inquiry requiring relevant evidence about access and other conditions.

How could early access shape later advancement, and what would you examine? Your reflection can remain private. Follow the reasoning from the immediate action to a possible repeated effect, then identify what would support or challenge that explanation.

slides.title: Another way to consider this
slides.text:
Another way to consider this

The case does not show who benefited by race or why. Naming a cause too soon can leave the invitation barrier unchanged. Trace how repeated early access becomes experience and recognition. Clarify the opportunity and compare evidence before claiming a racial pattern.

How could early access shape later advancement, and what would you examine?

Try another response

Continue learning
slides.narration:
The example does not identify who benefited by race or establish why. Declaring a cause prematurely can weaken the inquiry while leaving the actual invitation barrier unchanged. Trace how access becomes experience and later recognition, then compare appropriate evidence. Make the opportunity understandable and available while examining whether repetition contributes to racial advantage.

How could early access shape later advancement, and what would you examine? Your reflection can remain private. Follow the reasoning from the immediate action to a possible repeated effect, then identify what would support or challenge that explanation.

slides.title: Another way to consider this
slides.text:
Another way to consider this

An informal invitation can restrict access without intended exclusion. Repeated access for the same employees may preserve an advantage in later advancement. Examine the route and compare clearer invitations and relevant criteria. A racial pattern needs evidence; intent alone cannot settle effects.

How could early access shape later advancement, and what would you examine?

Try another response

Continue learning
slides.narration:
An informal invitation can restrict access even without an announced intent to exclude. If the same employees repeatedly gain experience, later advancement may preserve that initial advantage. Examine the route and consequences, then compare clearer invitations and relevant criteria. Whether the pattern is racial requires evidence; stated intent alone cannot settle its effects.

How could early access shape later advancement, and what would you examine? Your reflection can remain private. Follow the reasoning from the immediate action to a possible repeated effect, then identify what would support or challenge that explanation.

slides.title: Reflection: access to opportunity
slides.text:
Reflection: access to opportunity

A development opportunity reaches a familiar circle before other employees hear about it.

The information gap is visible. A racial pattern needs evidence about access, selection, and relevant circumstances.

Trace the path from invitation to experience, recognition, advancement, and retention.
slides.narration: Start with the action you can see: information was shared unevenly. Earlier access may make preparation and participation easier. The resulting experience can then be cited in a later advancement decision, making the original invitation disappear from the explanation. If this route repeats, opportunity may stay within the same network. Whether that pattern reflects racial advantage requires appropriate evidence about the people reached, selection criteria, and other conditions. You can compare the route without presuming the answer. Making the opportunity visible, explaining relevant criteria, and considering support are possible improvements; examining participation afterward can show what barriers remain.

slides.title: The effect of an ordinary practice
slides.text:
The effect of an ordinary practice

A service process assumes people can find information, interpret unfamiliar terms, and obtain help through established contacts.

Those assumptions may place extra effort or delay on people outside familiar networks.

Whose experience would help examine a racial barrier, and how could the process change in response?
slides.narration: A requirement may look simple from inside the organization because staff know its language and connections. For a person outside that network, the same step may require repeated calls, additional help, or an unanswered question. Those effects can accumulate through a whole service journey. Race, disability, language, income, and location may interact, and one account cannot establish how much each contributes. A culture brief can prepare you to ask about context. Community engagement brings particular experience into the inquiry. Compare the actual steps, hear what people encounter, and consider an alternative that preserves the necessary purpose while reducing an avoidable burden.

slides.title: Advantage and hardship
slides.text:
Advantage and hardship

Racial advantage can coexist with poverty, disability, loss, and other hardship.

Effort and hardship matter; they do not settle whether a particular racial barrier also exists.

Keep the specific service or workforce practice in view instead of ranking people’s lives.
slides.narration: Acknowledging hardship makes the inquiry more accurate and humane. It leaves room to ask a separate question: did race change a barrier in this particular situation? A person may encounter inaccessible documents and financial pressure while still receiving a benefit of the doubt not equally available to someone else. Neither experience erases the other. Turning the exchange into a contest over hardship can stop the racial concern from being examined. When that habit repeats, some barriers remain outside the organization’s explanation. Recognize the person’s experience, return to the practice, and identify what evidence would clarify how access or treatment differs.

slides.title: Practice: whose voice receives credit?
slides.text:
Practice: whose voice receives credit?

A colleague of color raises a policy concern. It receives attention only after a white colleague repeats it.

Acknowledge the original contribution and invite the colleague’s own explanation.

Consider how repeated losses of credit could affect influence, development, and advancement.

A response in the moment

“That returns to the concern our colleague raised earlier. Let’s hear their perspective.”

Restore credit now; examine the pattern with relevant evidence.
slides.narration: In this practice situation, the sequence is known, while the full explanation is not. Returning credit addresses the visible concern without announcing a conclusion about anyone’s beliefs. If the pattern repeats, one person’s knowledge may become less visible while another gains a reputation for insight. That can influence performance recognition and advancement. In community engagement, the same problem can occur when a professional receives credit for a concern first raised by people affected. Examine whose account receives attention and what happens to it in the decision. Race and role both deserve inquiry; one exchange does not establish their relative contribution.

slides.title: Support through everyday practice
slides.text:
Support through everyday practice

Listen to the concern and recognize the contribution or barrier described.

Make opportunities and criteria understandable, restore credit, and examine who can participate.

Ask whether changing the routine could prevent the same barrier from recurring.
slides.narration: A useful response changes something specific. You might return a conversation to its original contributor, clarify selection criteria, or make an invitation easier to find. Consider what follows from the action. Does the person now have room to explain their concern? Can someone outside the familiar network pursue the opportunity? A response in the moment matters, but a recurring pattern may need changes to the surrounding practice. Community participation and workplace feedback help you examine whether that change is usable. Keep race visible where relevant, recognize other conditions, and avoid treating a helpful first step as evidence that every barrier is resolved.

slides.title: Practice: community knowledge and influence
slides.text:
Practice: community knowledge and influence

People affected by a service change raise racial access concerns. The team responds only after a familiar professional repeats them. What would help?

A. Ask participants to disclose personal harm before considering the concern.

B. Move on because the concern was eventually discussed.

C. Recognize the original contribution, invite clarification, and examine how the team assigns credibility.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Ask participants to disclose personal harm before considering the concern.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Move on because the concern was eventually discussed.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Recognize the original contribution, invite clarification, and examine how the team assigns credibility.

slides.narration:
People affected by a service change raise racial access concerns. The team responds only after a familiar professional repeats them. What would help?

Choose a response, then read its explanation. Before choosing, consider the action described, the barrier or advantage it could create, and what might happen if the same response became routine. Keep the facts provided separate from the evidence still needed. You can reconsider your choice after reading the feedback.

slides.title: Another way to consider this
slides.text:
Another way to consider this

Requiring harm disclosure could silence knowledge of a service barrier. Repeated as a threshold, it may keep racial concerns out while favoring professional accounts. Consider the concern without requiring disclosure and invite clarification by choice. A wider racial pattern still needs evidence.

How would you check whose knowledge shaped the final service decision?

Try another response

Continue learning
slides.narration:
Requiring personal harm disclosure can prevent people from contributing knowledge about a service barrier. If repeated, that threshold can keep racial concerns out of decisions while favoring professional accounts. Consider the issue and evidence without requiring disclosure, and invite clarification by choice. The single exchange does not establish the full racial pattern or its cause.

How would you check whose knowledge shaped the final service decision? Your reflection can remain private. Follow the reasoning from the immediate action to a possible repeated effect, then identify what would support or challenge that explanation.

slides.title: Another way to consider this
slides.text:
Another way to consider this

Eventual discussion does not restore original credit or influence. Repeated credit to intermediaries can give professionals authority while community knowledge stays less visible. Recognize the original account and examine its influence. How race and professional status contributed remains unknown.

How would you check whose knowledge shaped the final service decision?

Try another response

Continue learning
slides.narration:
Eventually discussing the concern does not restore its original attribution or influence. Repeatedly crediting an intermediary could give professionals more authority while community knowledge remains less visible. Acknowledge the original account and examine how it affected the choice. The case raises questions about racial credibility and professional status; their contribution needs evidence.

How would you check whose knowledge shaped the final service decision? Your reflection can remain private. Follow the reasoning from the immediate action to a possible repeated effect, then identify what would support or challenge that explanation.

slides.title: Why this response helps
slides.text:
Why this response helps

Restore credit and invite clarification so people affected can explain their knowledge. A repeated credibility discount could exclude it from service design and preserve racial barriers. Compare how accounts enter decisions and improve that route. This exchange alone does not prove a wider racial pattern.

How would you check whose knowledge shaped the final service decision?

Continue learning
slides.narration:
Restoring attribution and inviting clarification returns room for people affected to explain their knowledge. A repeated credibility discount could exclude that knowledge from service design and preserve racial barriers. Compare how accounts enter decisions and consider a more consistent route for evidence. This response addresses the visible exchange without claiming that it proves a broader racial pattern.

How would you check whose knowledge shaped the final service decision? Your reflection can remain private. Follow the reasoning from the immediate action to a possible repeated effect, then identify what would support or challenge that explanation.

slides.title: Learning and follow-through
slides.text:
Learning and follow-through

Choose a specific service or workforce practice and identify what remains unknown.

Use culture briefs to prepare questions and hear from people affected.

The Equity Analysis Toolkit can help compare evidence, racial barriers, alternatives, and a supported next step.
slides.narration: You may begin with a question about whose concerns shape a service, how opportunities are shared, or what a person needs to navigate a process. Keep the inquiry small enough to examine clearly. A brief offers context, while people’s accounts may change how you understand the question. Look beyond whether input was collected: what happened to it, and could it influence an open choice? The toolkit supports a broader examination when several decisions or steps are connected. Work within your responsibility, retain appropriate permissions and privacy, and seek guidance where useful. A supported proposal explains the barrier, the reasoning behind the alternative, and what remains uncertain.

slides.title: Practice: a fairer invitation
slides.text:
Practice: a fairer invitation

An open development notice replaces informal invitations, but employees still find its criteria unclear.

Distribution is only one part of access; unclear criteria can preserve the original advantage.

What explanation and follow-up would help show whether people previously overlooked can use the opportunity?
slides.narration: The team has changed the invitation route, but the information may still assume background knowledge held by the earlier circle. If only familiar employees can interpret the criteria, the same opportunity pattern could continue under an apparently open process. Compare an explanation that makes relevant experience understandable and identifies how to express interest. Then examine who could participate and what difficulties remained. Recruitment, onboarding, mentoring, supervision, and retention can each supply different parts of the account. Use appropriate evidence and protect privacy. A revised notice is a useful output, while its actual effect on access and racial advantage remains a question to examine.

slides.title: Continuing the learning
slides.text:
Continuing the learning

Choose a service or employee-life-cycle practice for closer examination.

Describe an action, its possible barrier or advantage, and what repetition could sustain.

Keep race visible alongside disability and other circumstances; use community knowledge and evidence to consider a useful response.
slides.narration:
You have examined how racial advantage can travel through ordinary credibility judgments, information routes, and opportunities. For your next reflection, choose one practice you can understand more carefully. What action occurs? What does it make easier or harder? If it repeats, how might it influence service access, development, recognition, or retention? Identify whose experience could add to the account and what evidence would test your explanation. Personal understanding is worthwhile, and an appropriate work question can connect the learning with practice. One DSD brings culture briefs, community engagement, accessibility, and equity analysis together to support that continued inquiry. You do not need to settle every systemic issue to take a thoughtful next step.

Distinguish a possible racial mechanism from a conclusion requiring further evidence.
Describe a fairer opportunity without asking an affected person to prove the whole concept.
